_about: Weird and wonderful conditions (food poisonings, odd syndromes, strange colours and smells) for puzzle writers: Triviosis, Grand Rounds, Zebritis, Dxtective, Cryptogenic clues. Each item is a checked core fact; write all puzzle wording fresh and re-check details before publishing. Tone: fascinated, never mocking patients. Mark items used with "used": "YYYY-MM-DD game".

items.name: Scombroid fish poisoning
items.fact: Histamine from badly stored tuna or mackerel causes flushing, a peppery taste and hives within an hour. Cooking doesn’t destroy histamine; it isn’t an allergy.

items.name: Ciguatera
items.fact: Reef-fish toxin (ciguatoxin) from algae concentrates up the food chain. Classic sign: cold things feel hot (temperature reversal). Symptoms can linger for months.

items.name: Tetrodotoxin (fugu)
items.fact: Pufferfish toxin blocks sodium channels, causing numbness then paralysis with a clear mind. Licensed fugu chefs in Japan train for years. Also in blue-ringed octopus.

items.name: Paralytic shellfish poisoning
items.fact: Saxitoxin from algal blooms concentrates in mussels and oysters; tingling lips then paralysis. Cooking doesn’t help; shellfish beds are closed during blooms.

items.name: Honey intoxication (mad honey)
items.fact: Grayanotoxin in honey from some rhododendrons (notably Turkey’s Black Sea region) causes slow heart rate and low blood pressure. Used against Pompey’s soldiers in 67 BC.

items.name: Ackee poisoning
items.fact: Unripe ackee fruit (Jamaica’s national fruit) contains hypoglycin A, causing severe low blood sugar: ‘Jamaican vomiting sickness’.

items.name: Favism
items.fact: Broad (fava) beans trigger red cell breakdown in G6PD deficiency, the world’s most common enzyme deficiency. Pythagoras reputedly forbade his followers to eat beans.

items.name: Cassava konzo
items.fact: Poorly processed bitter cassava releases cyanide; in droughts it causes konzo, a sudden permanent leg paralysis seen in parts of Africa.

items.name: Bracken and potato green toxicity
items.fact: Green potatoes contain solanine; large amounts cause gut upset and confusion. Peel and discard green or sprouting parts.

items.name: Liquorice hypertension
items.fact: Glycyrrhizin in real liquorice blocks an enzyme protecting the kidney from cortisol, causing high blood pressure and low potassium. Black jelly-bean binges have caused heart rhythm problems.

items.name: Nutmeg intoxication
items.fact: Two tablespoons or more of nutmeg (myristicin) can cause hallucinations, a racing heart and a miserable day. Peaks hours after eating.

items.name: Beer potomania
items.fact: Drinking lots of beer with little food lowers sodium dangerously because the kidneys can’t excrete enough free water without solute.

items.name: Auto-brewery syndrome
items.fact: Gut yeast or bacteria ferment carbohydrates into alcohol, causing drunkenness without drinking. Has been used as a defence in drink-driving cases.

items.name: Carotenaemia
items.fact: Lots of carrots, pumpkin or sweet potato turn palms and soles orange-yellow, but not the whites of the eyes (unlike jaundice). Harmless.

items.name: Argyria
items.fact: Colloidal silver supplements permanently turn skin blue-grey. Famous ‘blue man’ cases followed home-made silver tonics.

items.name: Methaemoglobinaemia
items.fact: Some drugs (dapsone, topical benzocaine) or inherited enzyme defects make blood chocolate-brown and skin blue. The ‘Blue Fugates’ of Kentucky carried an inherited form. Treated with methylene blue.

items.name: Purple urine bag syndrome
items.fact: Catheter bags turn purple when gut bacteria and certain urine bacteria break down tryptophan products to indigo and indirubin, usually in constipated, catheterised older people.

items.name: Green urine from propofol
items.fact: Propofol and amitriptyline, among others, can turn urine green. Alarming, but harmless.

items.name: Beeturia
items.fact: About 1 in 10 people pass pink or red urine after eating beetroot, more often with iron deficiency.

items.name: Asparagus urine smell
items.fact: Asparagusic acid breaks down into sulfur compounds that make urine smell. Some people can’t smell it, due to a genetic variant.

items.name: Foreign accent syndrome
items.fact: A stroke or brain injury changes speech rhythm so a person sounds foreign. First described in 1907; a famous case was a Norwegian woman hit by shrapnel in 1941 who sounded German.

items.name: Exploding head syndrome
items.fact: A loud bang heard while falling asleep or waking, with no pain. Harmless and surprisingly common.

items.name: Alice in Wonderland syndrome
items.fact: Distorted perception of body size or objects (things look tiny or huge), most often with migraine or Epstein-Barr virus in children.

items.name: Capgras delusion
items.fact: Belief that a loved one has been replaced by an identical impostor. Linked to a disconnect between face recognition and emotional response.

items.name: Cotard delusion
items.fact: Belief that one is dead or lacks organs or blood. Named after Jules Cotard, 1880; usually with severe depression or psychosis, and treatable.

items.name: Alien hand syndrome
items.fact: One hand acts on its own, e.g. unbuttoning a shirt the other hand is buttoning. Seen after corpus callosum or frontal lobe damage.

items.name: Synaesthesia
items.fact: Senses blend: letters have colours, music has shapes. Found in a few per cent of people; often runs in families.

items.name: Brain freeze
items.fact: Sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia: cold on the palate triggers rapid blood vessel changes and referred headache. Pressing the tongue to the roof of the mouth helps.

items.name: Photic sneeze reflex
items.fact: ACHOO syndrome: sneezing when moving into bright light, found in roughly 1 in 5 to 1 in 4 people; inherited as a dominant trait.

items.name: Hiccups (singultus)
items.fact: Charles Osborne hiccupped for 68 years (1922–1990), a world record. Persistent hiccups can signal stroke, tumours or medicines.

items.name: Fish odour syndrome
items.fact: Trimethylaminuria: an enzyme (FMO3) defect leaves breath, sweat and urine smelling of rotting fish. Diet low in choline helps.

items.name: Maple syrup urine disease
items.fact: An inherited inability to break down branched-chain amino acids makes urine smell sweet like maple syrup. Found on newborn screening.

items.name: Stone man syndrome
items.fact: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva: muscles and tendons slowly turn to bone. Injury or surgery can trigger new bone. About 1 in 2 million people.

items.name: Hypertrichosis
items.fact: ‘Werewolf syndrome’: excessive hair growth over the body, inherited or acquired; the Gonzales family of the 1500s inspired ‘Beauty and the Beast’ tales.

items.name: Pica
items.fact: Craving non-food items. Pagophagia, chewing ice, is a strong clue to iron deficiency and often stops with iron.

items.name: Geophagia
items.fact: Eating soil or clay, seen in pregnancy and iron deficiency in many cultures.

items.name: Stendhal syndrome
items.fact: Dizziness, palpitations or fainting when overwhelmed by great art; named after the writer’s 1817 visit to Florence.

items.name: Paris syndrome
items.fact: Severe disappointment and anxiety on visiting Paris, described mostly in Japanese tourists.

items.name: Jerusalem syndrome
items.fact: Religious delusions triggered by visiting Jerusalem. (Keep puzzle wording neutral and non-religious in tone.)

items.name: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
items.fact: ‘Broken heart syndrome’: sudden heart muscle weakness after severe stress, mostly in older women. The heart balloons into the shape of a Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo).

items.name: Holiday heart syndrome
items.fact: Atrial fibrillation after binge drinking, classically after holiday weekends.

items.name: Saturday night palsy
items.fact: Radial nerve compression from sleeping with an arm draped over a chair, often after drinking: wrist drop.

items.name: Honeymoon cystitis
items.fact: Bladder infections linked to frequent sex. Passing urine after sex may help.

items.name: Gamekeeper’s thumb
items.fact: Ulnar collateral ligament injury of the thumb, originally from Scottish gamekeepers breaking rabbits’ necks; now ‘skier’s thumb’ from ski poles.

items.name: Housemaid’s knee
items.fact: Prepatellar bursitis from kneeling. Clergyman’s knee is the infrapatellar version.

items.name: Cherry red spot
items.fact: A red spot at the macula seen in central retinal artery occlusion and Tay-Sachs disease.

items.name: Heterochromia
items.fact: Different coloured eyes; can be inherited, from injury, or Horner syndrome in babies. David Bowie’s ‘different eyes’ were actually one permanently dilated pupil (anisocoria) from a fight.

items.name: Hiccup-cure vagal manoeuvres
items.fact: Swallowing sugar, holding breath and the ‘rectal massage’ cure (yes, in a published case report) all stimulate the vagus nerve.

items.name: Morgellons
items.fact: Belief that fibres emerge from the skin; studies find the fibres are cotton or other common materials. A form of delusional infestation; treat kindly.

starter_questions.q: Scombroid poisoning after eating tuna is caused by?
starter_questions.a: Histamine made by bacteria in poorly chilled fish
starter_questions.e: Fish rich in histidine (tuna, mackerel) let bacteria make histamine if not kept cold. Cooking doesn’t destroy it, and it isn’t an allergy.

starter_questions.q: Which clue points to scombroid rather than a fish allergy?
starter_questions.a: Several people who ate the same fish react together
starter_questions.e: Allergies are individual. A table of flushed diners points to histamine in the fish.

starter_questions.q: Eating ciguatera-contaminated reef fish can cause which odd symptom?
starter_questions.e: Temperature reversal is a classic sign of ciguatera, caused by ciguatoxin from algae concentrating up the reef food chain.

starter_questions.q: Orange palms but normal whites of the eyes after weeks of pumpkin soup suggest?
starter_questions.e: Carotene stains the skin but not the sclera, unlike jaundice. Harmless.

starter_questions.q: Chewing ice compulsively (pagophagia) is a classic clue to?
starter_questions.e: Pagophagia often resolves within days to weeks of iron treatment.
